strengths: The paper investigates an interesting and underexplored direction: whether the semantic/geometric priors encoded in a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model, together with human/VLM-generated captions, can help resolve monocular depth ambiguities (occlusion, small objects, textureless surfaces).

The paper provides a fairly extensive set of ablations: different denoising step counts, different caption-generation prompts, blank/template prompts as fallback when no user text is available, and stratified evaluation on small-area masks obtained via panoptic segmentation.

Qualitative visualizations (Figures 2, 4-6, 10-11) are informative and give an intuitive, consistent story for where language conditioning helps (small, occluded, or low-contrast objects) and where it can hurt (Figure 9, incorrect captions).
The pipeline and diffusion formulation are described clearly and are easy to follow, and the paper honestly reports a failure case and limitation regarding dependence on caption quality.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains over the direct baseline (Marigold) are very small and often within the noise band implied by the paper's own re-implementation variance: e.g., Marigold* at 20k vs 30k iterations swings NYUv2 δ1 between 95.2 and 95.7 and ETH3D between 93.9 and 95.4, which is comparable to or larger than the reported improvement of PriorDiffusion over Marigold (Table 1). No variance/multiple-seed results are reported to substantiate that the improvements are statistically meaningful rather than run-to-run noise.

The main quantitative comparison (Table 1) omits comparison to the most directly relevant prior language-for-depth baselines discussed at length in Related Work (DepthCLIP, WorDepth, RSA), despite these being the closest competitors to the paper's central claim; only image-only affine-invariant baselines are compared, which is not the most informative test of the paper's contribution.

The comparison to Marigold is potentially unfair as an ablation of the core hypothesis: PriorDiffusion receives an additional input (a VLM-generated caption produced by a separate, likely more capable model, LLaVA v1.6) at both train and test time, which already encodes object identity/semantics extracted from the image itself. It is unclear how much of the improvement stems from genuine 'language prior learned during text-to-image pretraining' versus simply exploiting extra information leaked into the caption by a stronger auxiliary model that already 'sees' the small/occluded object. No controlled experiment isolates the pretrained diffusion prior from the informational content of the caption itself (e.g., no ablation with random/shuffled correct-object captions vs. purely generic scene descriptions with matched information content).

Technical novelty is limited: the method essentially conditions the existing Stable Diffusion U-Net cross-attention on captions in the same way as standard text-to-image generation, applied to the Marigold depth pipeline. No new architectural or training mechanism specific to depth-language fusion is proposed beyond using off-the-shelf CLIP text encoding, which is already common practice in the SD ecosystem and related dense-prediction papers cited (VPD, GeoWizard).

The claims of 'faster convergence' and 'fewer denoising steps' are demonstrated only on unspecified 'subsets' of KITTI/NYUv2 without describing subset size or statistical robustness, and could equally be explained by the model receiving strictly more conditioning information rather than specifically by a 'language prior' effect.

Robustness to caption quality/errors is only illustrated with a single qualitative failure case (Figure 9); no quantitative study of sensitivity to caption noise, omissions, or hallucinations across the evaluation sets is provided, which is important given the method's reliance on VLM-generated text at test time.

The method requires generating a language description at test time for every input image (via a VLM), which is a nontrivial additional inference-time dependency not required by baselines like Marigold; this added compute/complexity is not clearly factored into the reported efficiency claims (e.g., fewer diffusion steps) for a fair efficiency comparison.
Code is stated as 'to be released' but not available with the submission, limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

strengths: Well-motivated and reasonably novel idea: injecting language prior into a Stable-Diffusion-based affine-invariant monocular depth estimator, extending Marigold with text conditioning and building on the observation that text-to-image pretraining encodes geometric/spatial knowledge.

Fairly comprehensive empirical study: quantitative results on four zero-shot benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet), plus ablations on denoising steps, training convergence speed, prompt templates, and performance on small/occluded regions, all pointing in a consistent direction.

The practical efficiency claims (fewer training iterations to reach comparable/better accuracy than Marigold, fewer denoising steps at inference) are a genuinely useful contribution if they hold up, since diffusion-based depth models are otherwise costly to train and sample from.

Good qualitative analysis and visualizations (Figs. 4-6, 10-11) that intuitively illustrate where language helps: small/occluded/low-contrast objects, and a nice 'controllable depth' demonstration where adding descriptive clauses incrementally improves specific regions.

Reasonably transparent about limitations: acknowledges dependency on caption quality, shows a failure case with an intentionally wrong caption, and discusses fallback strategies (template prompts) when user text is unavailable, with supporting ablation (Table 5).
weaknesses: The quantitative improvements over the re-implemented Marigold baseline are small and often within a fraction of a percentage point (e.g., NYUv2 δ1: 96.0 vs 95.7-95.9; KITTI AbsRel: 10.4 vs 10.4-10.7), with no reported variance/multiple-seed results, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the claimed gains, especially since PriorDiffusion is compared mainly against the authors' own Marigold re-implementation rather than the officially reported Marigold numbers in some rows.

The paper's framing emphasizes 'human-provided language prior,' but all captions (both train and test) are generated automatically by LLaVA rather than from real users; the practical benefit demonstrated is closer to auxiliary VLM-caption conditioning than genuine user-in-the-loop guidance, and the real-world use case (humans describing new environments) is not actually tested.

The claimed efficiency advantage in training/inference does not account for the substantial upstream cost of generating captions (740 GPU-hours reported for caption generation alone), which is a nontrivial addition to the total compute budget and undercuts the 'faster training convergence' narrative if total pipeline cost is considered.

No direct quantitative comparison against the most closely related language-for-depth methods (WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) on the same benchmarks, despite these being discussed at length in related work; the paper only compares against vision-only affine-invariant baselines, leaving the relative benefit of language over other cheaper geometric priors (e.g., simple scale/shift correction) unclear.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance' is overstated given Table 1 shows several large-data methods (Depth Anything v2, DPT, GeoWizard) outperforming PriorDiffusion by a considerable margin on multiple datasets/metrics; the paper's actual contribution is being competitive within the <100K-image training regime, which should be stated more precisely.

The mechanistic explanation for why language accelerates convergence (that geometric information is 'condensed and low-dimensional' in text) is asserted rather than empirically substantiated with a dedicated analysis (e.g., ablating caption informativeness/length vs. convergence speed).

Robustness to noisy or incorrect language is only illustrated with a single qualitative failure case; there is no systematic quantitative study of sensitivity to caption errors, omissions, or hallucinations, which is important given the model's real-world dependence on VLM-generated or user text.

Method is evaluated with a single backbone (Stable Diffusion v2) and single training scale (~74K images); no ablation studies generalization across backbones or larger training sets, so it is unclear whether the language-prior benefit persists or diminishes at larger scale.

strengths: Investigates a well-motivated and underexplored idea: using textual scene descriptions as an additional condition to reduce the ambiguity inherent to monocular depth estimation, framed around the plausible mechanism that text-to-image diffusion pretraining implicitly encodes 3D scene structure.

Broad empirical scope: the method is applied to three distinct diffusion-based depth estimators (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) and evaluated zero-shot on five real-world datasets (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, DIODE), which is a reasonably comprehensive testbed for this kind of ablation study.

The supplementary material contains useful ablations: sensitivity to caption-generation prompt, number of captions per image, use of fixed/template prompts when user text is unavailable, and behavior across different numbers of denoising steps.
Qualitative visualizations (Figures 2, 4-6, 10-11) are illustrative and support the intuitive story that text helps in regions that are small, occluded, or visually ambiguous.

The train-only vs. inference-only text ablation is an interesting analysis that probes whether language acts as a regularizer during training vs. as a runtime prior, offering some mechanistic insight beyond a simple main-result table.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains over baselines are frequently very small (often <1 point in δ1/AbsRel) and inconsistent across datasets/backbones, e.g., Lotus-G with train-only text on ETH3D substantially regresses (AbsRel 9.2→12.5) relative to its own re-trained baseline, undermining the claim of a robust, mechanism-driven improvement rather than training-run noise.

No repeated runs, variance estimates, or significance testing are reported despite baseline re-implementations (marked with *) already showing swings comparable in magnitude to the reported gains from adding text (e.g., Marigold* vs. Marigold), making it hard to confirm the improvements are attributable to language rather than stochastic training variation.

The paper does not include a control condition where an arbitrary/uninformative extra conditioning signal (e.g., a random or fixed embedding of the same dimensionality) is added instead of real captions, which would help isolate whether gains stem from the semantic content of language versus simply additional conditioning capacity/regularization.

Captions used at both train and test time are generated by the same or related VLMs conditioned on the image itself, raising a partial circularity concern: the model may be exploiting VLM-derived visual cues re-encoded as text rather than a genuinely independent language prior, which complicates interpreting the practical significance of the reported gains for real human-provided descriptions.

The paper does not compare against existing language-for-depth methods explicitly cited in related work (e.g., WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) as quantitative baselines, missing an opportunity to contextualize the magnitude of improvement relative to prior language-conditioned depth approaches.

Claims of 'faster convergence' and 'fewer denoising steps' are based on limited settings (a training subset for convergence curves, single-seed denoising-step sweeps), and the iterative refinement finding is supported only by a single qualitative example without a quantitative iterative-refinement metric.

Presentation issues remain, including leftover inconsistent naming ('PriorDiffusion' in supplementary figure captions vs. 'Iris' in the main text) and minor grammatical errors, suggesting the manuscript was not fully proofread.

Reliance on automatically generated captions for training/inference (VLM-based, not human-authored) somewhat undercuts the motivating narrative about human-provided language input for embodied agents, and the practical robustness to imperfect/ambiguous real descriptions is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation without deeper quantitative analysis beyond one qualitative failure case.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and interesting question: whether text conditioning learned during diffusion pre-training can be exploited to reduce ambiguity in monocular depth estimation, and it does so systematically across three different diffusion-based depth backbones (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) and five zero-shot evaluation benchmarks.

Extensive ablation studies are included: sensitivity to captioning prompts (Table 3), effect of denoising steps (Table 4/Fig. 8), behavior with fixed template prompts at inference (Table 5), and number of captions per image (Table 6), which is a level of experimental thoroughness beyond many workshop-style empirical studies.

Clear and intuitive qualitative visualizations (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 6, 9-11) that illustrate cases where text plausibly disambiguates small, occluded, or texture-ambiguous regions, aiding interpretability of the claimed mechanism.
The train-only vs. inference-only text ablation and the small-area evaluation (Table 2) are useful additional analyses that probe where and how the benefit of text arises.
The paper is candid about a clear failure mode (misleading text degrading predictions, Fig. 9), which is a reasonable and appropriately scoped limitation discussion.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains from integrating text are generally small (often 0.1-0.5 points in δ1/AbsRel) and inconsistent across datasets/backbones (e.g., Lotus-G+Text and E2E-FT+Text sometimes underperform their own original reported baselines in Table 1), and no error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The central causal claim -- that language provides a semantically grounded 3D scene prior that reduces the depth solution space -- is undercut by the paper's own ablation in Table 5, where blank or generic template prompts (with no scene-specific content) achieve performance comparable to or better than the trained model with actual descriptive captions. This suggests the observed gains may largely stem from a regularization effect of training with any text embedding rather than genuine semantic/geometric grounding, which is a significant tension with the paper's main narrative (Findings 1 and 2).

The evaluated setting requires a text description to be available at inference time for every test image, which is a nontrivial practical requirement that partly contradicts the premise of "monocular" (image-only) depth estimation; captions are generated by VLMs (LLaVA, InternVL3) rather than humans, raising a concern about information leakage from the VLM's own visual/geometric priors into the depth estimator, rather than a text-to-image diffusion prior being isolated as the source of improvement.

The method is a relatively direct combination of existing components (CLIP-conditioned diffusion U-Net + VLM-generated captions) applied to existing depth diffusion pipelines; while the empirical investigation is thorough, the technical/methodological novelty is modest relative to prior language-for-depth work (e.g., WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) and standard text-conditioned diffusion architectures.

There is a naming inconsistency between the main paper ("Iris") and the supplementary material, which repeatedly refers to the method as "PriorDiffusion" in figure captions, suggesting incomplete editing/proofreading and raising minor concerns about manuscript care.

The comparison table mixes originally reported baseline numbers with the authors' own re-trained/re-evaluated baselines (marked with *), and in some cases the "+Text" variants are compared favorably against the weaker reproduced baseline rather than the stronger originally published baseline, which could give a somewhat optimistic impression of the improvement.

No discussion of the added inference-time cost of running a VLM captioning step (in addition to the depth diffusion model), which is relevant to the claimed efficiency benefit from fewer denoising steps.
